P1-14.P1_flat: - Port buffers. A FIFO instance whose write data is a unit input port's value (a bus write, or bits shifted in from a serial input port) only buffers data between two ports. Its fill flags (holds data, has room, half full), push and pop strobes, a command used only to clear it, and a push-while-full flag (even a register of this unit) only time, gate, clear or report on that data: they are not pieces of their own, although step 2 would call some a decision; cite no line assigning or wiring them as a held line. Judged as usual: the buffered data, an output port these flags decide (an interrupt request, a ready-to-receive line), and a unit enable also clearing the FIFO. A FIFO holding data the unit generates rather than receives (random bits) is not covered: its holds-data flag that a statement of this unit tests to return either that data or something else (the flag withholds the data) and a register whose only use is to clear that FIFO (it discards the data) are each their own piece (step 2) that no step-3 clause folds into that data, the flag held at the line wiring it out of the FIFO, with the read-data line returning the flag as its exit (step 6), and the register held at the line assigning it, while its other flags and its push, pop and enable controls are judged as usual. Any FIFO instance, whatever data it holds, keeps each word only while the word moves (2.6: a copy kept only while the value moves), so the signals (not ports) wired to its write-data input and driven by its read-data output only carry the word and are not pieces of their own; the buffered data is judged where the unit generates it (random bits) or where it crosses the unit's boundary at a port. Cite no line assigning or wiring those two signals as a held line; leave "Held Lines" empty if no other line holds the data. Judge from port names that an instance is a FIFO, which outputs are its flags and which ports carry its data, and say so.

  Criteria: the FIFO's write data is a unit input port's value (a bus write, or bits shifted in from a serial input port).
  Exceptions: judged as usual: the buffered data, an output port these flags decide (an interrupt request, a ready-to-receive line), and a unit enable also clearing the FIFO; a FIFO holding data the unit generates rather than receives (random bits) is not covered.
  Outcome: not pieces of their own, although step 2 would call some a decision: the FIFO only buffers data between two ports; they only time, gate, clear or report on that data.
  Evidence: cite no line assigning or wiring them as a held line; judge from port names that an instance is a FIFO, which outputs are its flags and which ports carry its data, and say so.
- Port buffers (b).
  Scope: that FIFO (random bits).
  Criteria (any of): (1) its holds-data flag that a statement of this unit tests to return either that data or something else (the flag withholds the data); (2) a register whose only use is to clear that FIFO (it discards the data).
  Exceptions: judged as usual: its other flags and its push, pop and enable controls.

- Port buffers (c).
  Scope: any FIFO instance, whatever data it holds; signals (not ports).
  Criteria (any of): (1) wired to its write-data input; (2) driven by its read-data output.
  Outcome: the FIFO keeps each word only while the word moves (2.6: a copy kept only while the value moves); they only carry the word and are not pieces of their own; the buffered data is judged where the unit generates it (random bits) or where it crosses the unit's boundary at a port.
  Evidence: cite no line assigning or wiring those two signals as a held line; leave "Held Lines" empty if no other line holds the data.

P1-17.P1_flat: - Buffer and engine status bits. A status bit a bus read returns is not information of its own when every element it copies (even inverted) or combines is barred by this call's rule on a FIFO only buffering data between two ports (never a flag of a FIFO holding data the unit generates rather than receives) or on sequencing state (state register, counter, or busy or done flag derived from them): it only tells software whether the buffered or shifted data can move or was lost, which that data, its settings and the output ports these elements decide already cover. Although step 1 names status and 4.3 status signals, keep no concept for such bits, alone or grouped as the status software reads, and cite no read-data line returning them as a held line. Not covered: a bit returning anything else, even in the same read word (the buffered data, a stored setting, selection or lock, a reset's cause record); it belongs to the piece it returns, as that piece's exit (step 6). Not covered either: the output ports these elements decide (an interrupt request, a ready-to-receive line), a register a test or debug access port shifts out, and, in a unit executing instructions, the word an instance outputs for reads of its control and status registers.

P1-10.P1_flat: - Hand-offs. Check each port-map line where an instance's non-record output port drives a signal another instance or this unit's logic reads. A wait, fault or write-enable flag, or an access address, that one instance outputs on a non-record port to another instance or this unit's logic is a hand-off; if the RTL cannot show which it is, judge from the port names at either end and say so; a field of a record an instance outputs on a record port is never a hand-off, even wired alone into another instance's non-record port. A hand-off is its own piece (step 2), unless Port buffers covers it (then this rule does not apply). No step-3 clause or other rule folds it, even when it travels with the data it qualifies, when another instance outputs the same address earlier or later (cite each output's port-map line, in one piece), or when it is one bit of a count: then hold it at the line assigning that bit to the instance output, and a count kept only to make it belongs to this piece.
P1-10.P1_structured:
- Hand-offs.
  Scope: check each port-map line where an instance's non-record output port drives a signal another instance or this unit's logic reads; a wait, fault or write-enable flag, or an access address.
  Criteria: that one instance outputs on a non-record port to another instance or this unit's logic.
  Exceptions: a field of a record an instance outputs on a record port is never a hand-off, even wired alone into another instance's non-record port; if Port buffers covers it, then this rule does not apply.
  Outcome: a hand-off: its own piece (step 2). No step-3 clause or other rule folds it, even when it travels with the data it qualifies, when another instance outputs the same address earlier or later (cite each output's port-map line, in one piece), or when it is one bit of a count: then hold it at the line assigning that bit to the instance output, and a count kept only to make it belongs to this piece.
  Evidence: if the RTL cannot show which kind it is, judge from the port names at either end and say so.
P1-10.P2_flat: A wait, fault or write-enable flag, or an access address, that one instance outputs on a non-record port to another instance or this unit's logic is a hand-off; if the RTL cannot show which it is, judge from the port names at either end and say so; a field of a record an instance outputs on a record port is never a hand-off, even wired alone into another instance's non-record port. Label a hand-off primary for its conceptual asset where the instance outputs it: the output port of an instance of this file when this unit only wires that port into another instance, and otherwise the unit signal the port map drives; when another instance outputs the same address earlier or later, label each output. When a hand-off is one bit of a count, the line assigning that bit to the output is where it is computed: the count is not primary for that conceptual asset, and can be its secondary (2.7). Apart from the port-buffer bar on a FIFO, no bar in this step covers a hand-off.
